title: Design a Parking Lot
description: Walk through the classic OOP design problem — identify classes, relationships, and apply SOLID principles to build an extensible parking lot system.

segments.text: Welcome to low-level design. We're going to design a parking lot system from scratch. Sounds simple, right? It's deceptively deep — and it's the most common OOP interview question out there.
First, let's nail the requirements. Multiple floors, different vehicle types — cars, bikes, trucks. A ticket system for entry and exit. Payment processing. And real-time spot availability tracking.
Here's the trick for any LLD problem. Read the requirements and underline every noun. Parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, ticket — those are your candidate classes. Verbs become your methods.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you spot which nouns should become classes and which are just attributes?

segments.text: Let's start with Vehicle. It's an abstract base class — you never create a generic vehicle. You create a Car, a Bike, or a Truck. Each has a license plate and a vehicle type. Classic inheritance.

Next, ParkingSpot. Each spot has a size — small, medium, large. A small spot fits a bike, medium fits a car, large fits a truck. The spot tracks whether it's occupied and which vehicle is parked there.

The Floor class holds a collection of ParkingSpots. It knows how many spots of each type are available. When you need to park a vehicle, the floor searches for a compatible free spot. Composition over inheritance here.

ParkingLot is the top-level class. It contains multiple floors, manages entry and exit gates, and coordinates the whole system. This is the Facade pattern — one simple interface hiding complex internals.

The Ticket class captures the entry timestamp, assigned spot, vehicle reference, and payment status. When a vehicle exits, we calculate the fee based on duration. Strategy pattern works great for different pricing rules.

Now connect everything. ParkingLot HAS-A list of Floors. Floor HAS-A list of ParkingSpots. ParkingSpot HAS-A Vehicle when occupied. Ticket references both Vehicle and ParkingSpot. These are your composition relationships.

Let's check SOLID. Single Responsibility — each class does one thing. Open-Closed — add EV charging spots without modifying existing code. Liskov — any Vehicle subclass works where Vehicle is expected. This design is clean.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you add handicapped parking spots without changing existing classes?

segments.text: Need EV charging? Create an ElectricSpot subclass. Handicapped spots? Another subclass. Different payment methods? Strategy pattern. The beauty of good OOP is that new features are additions, never modifications.

That's the parking lot design. Remember the process: gather requirements, identify nouns as classes, define relationships, then validate against SOLID. This same approach works for any LLD problem you'll face in interviews.
